 Medicare Advantage withdrawals leave thousands of Whidbey residents seeking new coverage
 Published 1:30 am Friday, November 6, 2026
 By Cassandra Diamond cassandra.diamond@whidbeynewsgroup.com 
 Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... 
 Several insurance providers have pulled their individual Medicare Advantage plans from Island County, leaving thousands of local beneficiaries facing the prospect of changing health insurance, finding new doctors and navigating unfamiliar coverage options.
 Kaiser Permanente and Wellcare are no longer offering individual Medicare Advantage plans for county residents in 2027. According to Annette Barca, a Statewide Health Insurance Benefits Advisors program volunteer coordinator with Island Senior Resources, UnitedHealthcare has also pulled some of its Medicare Advantage plans from Island County.
 While she doesn’t have an exact count, Barca estimated that well over 3,000 seniors have lost their Medicare Advantage plans for the coming year. The large number of affected beneficiaries has strained the resources of local insurance advisers and agents.
 The withdrawals limit available options during the annual Medicare open enrollment period, which started Oct. 15 and ends Dec. 7. Those whose plans are being discontinued also qualify for a special enrollment period extending through Feb. 28, 2027, giving them additional time to select replacement coverage.
 Medicare Advantage, also known as Medicare Part C, is an “all-in-one” alternative to original Medicare offered by private insurance companies. Beneficiaries whose plans are discontinued do not lose Medicare itself, but they may need to find new coverage and doctors.
 Insurance Whidbey owner and agent Naomi DeMartini explained that the withdrawals are primarily driven by “business decisions.” In rural areas such as Island County, factors such as the cost and use of medical care influence whether insurers consider their plans financially sustainable. Companies are not required to offer plans in every county.
 “It’s a tough environment right now,” DeMartini said. “So if companies see that they’re not in areas where they’re able to be sustainable, they will pull out.”
 Barca noted that Kaiser has been reducing its number of out-of-network providers eligible for coverage over time, effectively eliminating local provider options on Whidbey. She attributed the company’s withdrawal from the county’s individual Medicare Advantage market to the lack of available providers on the island.
 DeMartini said the situation is even worse for those who chose to receive their care at Kaiser facilities, as they are not only losing their current insurance plans but potentially access to their primary doctors as well.
 She emphasized that while Island County has been hit several times by reductions like these over the last few years, this is “one of the biggest” she has seen in more than 12 years in the insurance industry.
 The situation has caused significant unrest and fear for Island County Medicare beneficiaries, DeMartini said, as many of those affected have been on the same health care plan for upwards of 15 years.
 “With what’s happening right now, people are having to change their plans more often, which can be really difficult,” she said. “Especially as we get older and have more providers, it becomes more complex to find a plan that’s a good fit.”
 Barca echoed this sentiment, noting that many seniors whose plans are ending now face uncertainty about what options are available, how much new coverage will cost, whether they can keep their doctors and how they will get to appointments if they must travel farther for care.
 Both DeMartini and Barca said the large number of affected beneficiaries has stretched their respective organizations’ resources thin.
 In particular, Barca said SHIBA volunteers on Whidbey have been working overtime to help affected Medicare beneficiaries, with some putting in more than 40 hours a week.
 David de Wolf, an Island Senior Resources employee who helps support Barca and the SHIBA program, said SHIBA advisers have added several sessions this enrollment period specifically for people who have lost their Medicare Advantage plans.
 “The sheer numbers are overwhelming,” Barca said.
 DeMartini and Barca explained that those whose Medicare Advantage plans are ending have three main options.
 The first is to find and enroll in a different Medicare Advantage plan that is still available in Island County. The second is to return to original Medicare, which will happen automatically when their current plan ends if they do not enroll in another Medicare Advantage plan. Those who need prescription drug coverage may also need to enroll in a separate Medicare Part D plan.
 The third option is available to those who return to original Medicare and involves purchasing a Medicare supplement plan, also called Medigap, to help pay out-of-pocket costs. People whose Medicare Advantage plans are discontinued may qualify for guaranteed-issue rights, allowing them to purchase certain Medigap policies without being denied coverage or charged more because of pre-existing conditions. These protections have eligibility requirements and application deadlines.
 Barca added that the special enrollment period gives people affected by plan nonrenewals until Feb. 28 to select a new Medicare Advantage plan, although Medigap enrollment rights have separate deadlines.
 DeMartini also noted that Kaiser’s exit from individual Medicare Advantage plans will likely not affect its retirement Medicare Advantage plans. Beneficiaries should verify whether their specific plan is ending before making changes to avoid unnecessarily losing existing coverage.
 Above all, DeMartini urged Island County residents to reach out to their elected officials and the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services to make it clear the current situation is unacceptable.
 “I think that people need to speak up and let their elected representatives and those in the government know what’s going on,” she said. “Because if we don’t do that, we’re going to continue to see these types of things happening in our area, and it makes it harder for all of us.”
